title: A payoff is a function
objectives: Write a simple trading payoff as a piecewise function and draw its graph.
Shift a payoff by the premium to get the P&L and find the break-even.

screens.prose: A call option gives you the right, not the duty, to buy a share for £100.00 at expiry. If the share ends at £112.00, you buy at £100.00 and gain £12.00.
screens.question: What does the call pay if the share ends at £93.00?

hints.text: Would you choose to pay £100.00 for a share worth £93.00?
The row above shows the payoff at £100.00.
You let the right lapse, so the payoff is £0.00.

feedback.correct: £0.00: you simply do not use the right.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide whether you would choose to buy at £100.00.

byKey.neg: You worked out $93 - 100 = -7$. That means buying at £100.00 a share worth £93.00. You do not have to.
byKey.pos: You paid out the gap the other way round. A call pays only when the share ends above £100.00.

explain.text: Below £100.00 you walk away, so the payoff is £0.00. Above it, the payoff is $S - 100$, where $S$ is the share price at expiry. The payoff is two rules joined at £100.00.

screens.prose: Here is the payoff as a graph. The strike $K$ is the price you may buy at. Slide $K$ and drag P along the graph.
screens.question: Set $K = 105$. What does the call pay if the share ends at £112.00?

hints.text: With $K = 105$ you buy at £105.00.
Drag P to £112.00 and read its height.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the new strike from £112.00.

byKey.old: You used the old strike, £100.00. With $K = 105$ you buy at £105.00, so you gain £7.00.
byKey.strike: £105.00 is the strike. The payoff is what you gain: the share price minus the strike.

explain.text: The payoff is $112 - 105 = 7$. Moving $K$ slides the kink sideways and nothing else: a horizontal shift. Left of $K$ the graph is flat at 0; right of it, it rises £1.00 per £1.00.

screens.prose: A rule made of different pieces on different intervals is a **piecewise function**. The call payoff with $K = 100$ is $$C(S) = \begin{cases} 0 & S \le 100 \\ S - 100 & S > 100 \end{cases}$$
screens.question: On each piece, how much does the payoff rise when $S$ rises by £1.00?

options.text: £0.00 on the left piece, £1.00 on the right piece
£1.00 on the left piece, £1.00 on the right piece
options.why: You used the gradient of $S - 100$ everywhere. The left piece is the constant 0, so it does not rise.

options.text: £0.00 on the left piece, £100.00 on the right piece
options.why: You read the 100 as a gradient. In $S - 100$ the gradient is the 1 in front of $S$; the 100 only shifts the line.

hints.text: What are the gradients of $y = 0$ and $y = S - 100$?
Compare the flat part with the rising part.
$y = 0$ is flat: gradient 0. $y = S - 100$ has gradient 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the gradient of each piece separately.

explain.text: The left piece, 0, is flat. The right piece, $S - 100$, has gradient 1. The kink at £100.00 is where the rule changes.

screens.prose: A put gives the right to sell at $K = 100$. It pays $100 - S$ if the share ends below £100.00, and nothing above.
screens.question: Drag the control points to sketch the put's payoff from £80.00 to £120.00.

hints.text: What does the put pay at £80.00, £100.00 and £120.00?

feedback.correct: High on the left, falling to 0 at the strike, flat after.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the payoff at each control point, then place it there.

byKey.call: You drew the call's payoff. A put pays when the share ends below the strike, so it is high on the left.

explain.text: The put pays $100 - S$ below £100.00: £20.00 at £80.00, falling to 0 at the strike. Above £100.00 it is flat at 0. It is the call reflected in the vertical line $S = 100$.

screens.prose: You paid a premium of £4.00 for the call with $K = 100$. Your profit and loss is the payoff shifted down by 4: $C(S) - 4$.
screens.question: At what share price do you break even?

hints.text: Where does the P&L line cross zero?
Only the rising piece can reach zero.
On the right piece the P&L is $S - 100 - 4$. Set it to 0.

byKey.kink: At £100.00 the payoff is 0, so the P&L is −£4.00.
byKey.minus: You took the premium off the strike. The call gains as the share rises, so it needs £4.00 above the strike.

explain.text: On the right piece the P&L is $S - 100 - 4$, which is 0 at $S = 104$. The premium shifts the graph down 4. The rising piece then needs 4 more to reach zero.

screens.prose: Same call: strike £100.00, premium £4.00. The share collapses to £60.00. A colleague extends the rising line of the P&L leftwards and reads off a big loss.
screens.question: What is your P&L if the share ends at £60.00?

options.why: You extended the rising piece, $S - 104$, past the kink. Below £100.00 the flat piece applies, so you lose only the premium.
You used the payoff, which is 0. The £4.00 premium is spent either way.
You took the share's fall from £100.00 to £60.00 as your loss. You never buy the share, so its fall costs you nothing more.

hints.text: Which piece of the rule covers $S = 60$?
The graph stops at £90.00; carry on with the flat piece.
Below £100.00 the payoff is 0, so the P&L is $0 - 4$.

feedback.correct: −£4.00: the loss stops at the premium.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the piece that covers prices below £100.00.

byKey.extend: You carried the rising piece below the kink. That piece only holds for $S > 100$; below it the P&L is flat.
byKey.nopremium: The payoff is 0, but you paid £4.00 for the option. The P&L is the payoff minus the premium.
byKey.gap: The fall in the share is not your loss. You hold the right to buy, and you simply do not use it.

explain.text: Below the strike the call is not used, so the payoff is 0 and the P&L is $0 - 4 = -4$. However far the share falls, the loss stops at the premium. Each piece of a piecewise function holds only on its own interval.

screens.prose: A digital option pays £10.00 if the share ends above £100.00, and nothing otherwise. Its graph jumps. A filled dot belongs to its piece; an open dot does not.
screens.question: What does the digital pay if the share ends at exactly £100.00?

hints.text: Look at the two dots at £100.00.
The filled dot is on the lower piece, at £0.00.

feedback.correct: £0.00: the filled dot is on the lower piece.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check which dot at £100.00 is filled.

byKey.ten: You used the upper piece. Its dot at £100.00 is open: that piece starts just above £100.00.
byKey.half: You split the difference. A function gives one output at each input, here the filled dot.

explain.text: 'Above £100.00' leaves out 100 itself, so the lower piece applies: £0.00. At a jump, the filled and open dots say which piece owns the boundary. 'Above' and 'at least' differ exactly here.

screens.prose: Each payoff was a rule in pieces. For a call and a put with strike $K$: $$C(S) = \max(S - K, 0) \qquad P(S) = \max(K - S, 0)$$ $\max$ picks the larger of the two, so it switches piece at $S = K$. The P&L subtracts the premium: a shift down.
screens.question: Which is the P&L of a put with strike 100 bought for £3.00?

options.why: You put the premium inside the max. Then the P&L could never go below 0, but the premium is lost when the put pays nothing.
That is the call's P&L. A put pays when $S$ is below 100.
You added the premium. You paid it, so it comes off the payoff.

hints.text: Start from the put payoff, then shift it down by the premium.

feedback.correct: Payoff first, then subtract the premium.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the put payoff, then shift it down by 3.

explain.text: The put payoff is $\max(100 - S, 0)$. Paying £3.00 shifts every output down 3. So the P&L is $\max(100 - S, 0) - 3$, never below −£3.00.

screens.prose: Find the break-even share price of a put with strike £100.00, bought for £3.00.
screens.question: Put the lines of the working in order.

lines.text: For $S \le 100$ the P&L is $100 - S - 3$: the payoff minus the premium
Set $100 - S - 3 = 0$: break-even means a P&L of zero
Check $97 \le 100$: we used the right piece

hints.text: Start by choosing the piece of the rule, then solve.
Piece, equation, simplify, solve, then check the answer lies on that piece.

feedback.correct: Break-even at £97.00, on the piece where the put pays.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose the piece first and check it last.

byKey.e: The check comes last: it tests the answer you found.
byKey.a: Start by writing the P&L on the piece where the put pays.

explain.text: On the paying piece the P&L is $97 - S$, which is 0 at $S = 97$. Since $97 \le 100$, that piece really applies. Always check a piecewise answer against the interval it came from.

screens.prose: A broker charges £9.95 per trade or 0.1% of the trade value, whichever is larger. For a trade of £$v$ the fee is $F(v) = \max(9.95, 0.001v)$.
screens.question: Above what trade value does the 0.1% piece take over?

hints.text: The pieces meet where $0.001v = 9.95$.
Find the kink in the graph.

byKey.percent: You divided by 0.01, which is 1%. 0.1% is 0.001, so $9.95 \div 0.001 = 9950$.
byKey.rounded: Close, but read it exactly: the pieces meet where $0.001v = 9.95$.

explain.text: The two pieces meet where $0.001v = 9.95$, at $v = 9950$. Below £9,950.00 the flat fee is larger; above it, 0.1% is. So a £15,000.00 trade costs £15.00.

ideas: A payoff uses a different rule on each side of the strike: it is a piecewise function.
$\max(S - K, 0)$ writes the call in one line; the P&L shifts it down by the premium.
At a jump, the filled dot shows which piece owns the boundary.

formula.name: Call and put payoffs
formula.note: Subtract the premium for the P&L of a bought option.

summary.trap: Do not extend a piece past its interval: below the strike a bought call loses only the premium.

quiz.prose: A call with strike £50.00 was bought for £2.50.
quiz.question: What is the P&L if the share ends at £56.00?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the payoff, then subtract the premium.

byKey.nopremium: £6.00 is the payoff. The premium you paid comes off it.
byKey.added: You added the premium. You paid it, so subtract it.

explain.text: The payoff is $56 - 50 = 6$. Subtracting the £2.50 premium gives a P&L of £3.50.

quiz.question: What does it pay if the share ends at £86.00?

feedback.correct: £0.00: you would not sell at £80.00 a share worth £86.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide which piece covers £86.00.

byKey.neg: You used $80 - S$ above the strike. That piece only holds below £80.00.

explain.text: Above the strike the put's payoff is $\max(80 - 86, 0) = 0$. You simply do not use the right to sell.

options.why: You used the first piece, $2x$. It holds only for $x < 3$, which leaves out 3.
A function gives one output. The sign $\ge$ puts 3 on the second piece.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find which piece includes $x = 3$.

explain.text: The second piece holds for $x \ge 3$, which includes 3. So $f(3) = 10 - 3 = 7$. This function jumps from just under 6 to 7.

quiz.prose: A fee is $\max(5, 0.002v)$ pounds on a trade of £$v$.
quiz.question: What is the fee on a £1,800.00 trade?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out both pieces and take the larger.

byKey.percent: £3.60 is the percentage piece. The max takes the larger of 5 and 3.60.

explain.text: The percentage piece gives £3.60 and the flat piece £5.00. $\max$ picks the larger, so the fee is £5.00. Small trades pay the floor.
